title: Wei
capsule: Wei (魏) was one of the Three Jins, the successor states formed when the ministerial Wei, Han, and Zhao clans partitioned the state of Jin, a division formally recognized by the Zhou king in 403 BCE. Under its first sovereign, Marquess Wen of Wei (r. 445–396 BCE), it became the earliest dominant power of the Warring States, employing the statesman Li Kui to codify laws and reform agriculture and the general Wu Qi to build a disciplined army. Centered first on its capital at Anyi in the Fen and Yellow River valleys, Wei later shifted its seat eastward to Daliang (modern Kaifeng) as Qin pressed in from the west; the disastrous defeat at the Battle of Maling (341 BCE) against Qi broke its hegemony. The state was steadily reduced thereafter and was finally extinguished in 225 BCE when the Qin general Wang Ben breached the dikes of the Yellow River to flood Daliang.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Cao Wei's territory in northern China is well documented by the administrative geography of its commandery system, itself inherited from the Han census; the fluctuating southern frontiers contested with Shu Han and Eastern Wu are attested by campaign records but are imprecisely rendered as fixed lines.
